messages.author: 6db62e08ec862130
messages.subject: 2 kinds of error checking
parts:
I find with a perusal of the source code that there are two kinds of
error checks.

+ Checks that only need to be done once to verify that the model can be
evaluated (like matrix conformability checking).

+ Checks that need to be done at every iteration (like checking whether
a covariance matrix is positive definite).

Currently, it appears that both of these types of checks are done at
every iteration. Do we have a plan to split up these checks into
separate parts of the generated source code?

--
Joshua N. Pritikin

messages.author: cab04b8f0759c712
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] 2 kinds of error checking
parts:
Hi Joshua,

We're thinking about it the same way. There's an issue open for this:
https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/685

and a pull request that addresses it:
https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/pull/1207

The pull request only changes what's being thrown, there's no change in behavior, yet.

On Thu, Jan 22, 2015 at 8:35 AM, Joshua N Pritikin <jpri...@pobox.com> wrote:
I find with a perusal of the source code that there are two kinds of
error checks.

+ Checks that only need to be done once to verify that the model can be
evaluated (like matrix conformability checking).

+ Checks that need to be done at every iteration (like checking whether
a covariance matrix is positive definite).

Currently, it appears that both of these types of checks are done at
every iteration. Do we have a plan to split up these checks into
separate parts of the generated source code?

We've thought about splitting it up, but not in the generated source code. There really isn't much in the generated code that needs to be separated.

If we were to split it up, one way to do it would be to add a bool template parameter that indicates whether checks that can be done once needs to be done. Of course, this isn't fool-proof: since Stan has conditionals, we might run into a problem if we branched differently later.

Even if we didn't split apart the checking, with the pull request, we'll be able to handle the errors differently, which would improve the behavior of Stan for the users. We'd be able to stop immediately after catching one of the first types of errors.



With that said, we've gone back and forth about trying to turn off checking. Most of the checks are fast and you won't notice the impact of removing checks like checking matrix sizes, checking nan, etc. (well... after the pull request that's one now that fixes the std::string issue) There are a few checks that are slow and can use some work. One reason for not doing what I suggested above is that it adds complexity to our code. A lot of complexity. Unless we have a lot of speed benefit, I don't think we should go down this path. If you or anyone can show that these actually have an large impact on models, then I'm all ears.



Daniel

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] 2 kinds of error checking
parts:
On Thu, Jan 22, 2015 at 10:35 AM, Joshua N Pritikin <jpri...@pobox.com> wrote:
On Thu, Jan 22, 2015 at 10:20:12AM -0500, Daniel Lee wrote:
>    Unless we have a lot of speed benefit, I don't think we should go
>    down this path. If you or anyone can show that these actually have
>    an large impact on models, then I'm all ears.

I certainly don't have benchmarking numbers. I agree that any impact is
likely to be difficult to measure.

I remember going through the exercise of removing the check_nan's from all our code to find that there was no observable impact to our Stan programs. I believe profilers showed that function taking 15% of the time.

If there was an impact, I'd do something about it, so if you're able to show a performance hit, let me know.

>      Do we have a plan to split up these checks into
>      separate parts of the generated source code?
>
>    If we were to split it up, one way to do it would be to add a bool
>    template parameter that indicates whether checks that can be done once
>    needs to be done. Of course, this isn't fool-proof: since Stan has
>    conditionals, we might run into a problem if we branched differently
>    later.

Why wouldn't you structure it as a separate function like

    template <bool propto, typename T_y, typename T_loc, typename T_covar>
    void multi_normal_log_preflight(const T_y& y, const T_loc& mu,
                   const Eigen::MatrixBase<T_covar>& Sigma) {
        // conformability checking here
    }

?

=). Great suggestion, but there are at least a couple issues:

1) I don't trust programmers to do the right thing if it requires taking an additional step (this includes me!). I can already see where this would lead -- we'd be hunting down bugs where the preconditions weren't validated (we'd have to explicitly write down all preconditions for all functions first), then our functions will get into undefined behavior, and we're just going to have to dig deep to find bugs. Personally, I think the way we do it now reduces programmer time significantly. No need to search for where the checks are, when conditions are violated, etc.

2) It'd be great if we were in a language where there was reflection, but we're not. I don't think we can implement inversion of control in a general way where each of these functions calls a "preflight" function that's defined outside. If there was, I'd be all for putting the different checks into different cross-cutting layers.

>    With that said, we've gone back and forth about trying to turn off
>    checking. Most of the checks are fast and you won't notice the impact
>    of removing checks like checking matrix sizes, checking nan, etc.

Sure, but we might be willing to check more costly things if the checks
were only run once.

Examples? If you've got a compelling use-case, we can give it some real thought. I prefer not over-engineering based on potential uses.




Daniel

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] 2 kinds of error checking
parts:
Thanks for bringing the discussion onto stan-dev.

The most time consuming checks are the ones that test things
like positive-definiteness of a matrix or even symmetry.
For data, these are done only once. For parameters, they
have to be done every iteration.

It's technically impossible to pre-check with our current language,
but explaining why is a bit of digression into CS theory.

Because Stan is Turing complete (a consequence of having
general while loops and assignment), it's impossible to
figure out even whether a statement will get executed (the
problem is technically what is known as "undecidable" in
computational theory).

Without worrying about really hard cases, consider
this program:

parameters {
real<lower=0,upper=1> theta;
...

model {
int n;
if (theta > 0.99)
n <- 20;
else
n <- 10;
...
tail(y,n) ~ normal(tail(mu,n), sigma);

the problem is that whether the call to normal is sound or not
depends on a run-time choice based on the value of theta. So it
can't just be done once.

Similarly, we have a requirement that sigma > 0, but due to
problems with floating point underflow, we can wind up with sigma == 0
on some iterations. So those tests have to remain at runtime.

Now the problem is that you'd think indexing would be checkable
ahead of time, but now the index depends on a parameter. Whether the
tail statement and hence the normal are well formed will depend on
n.

We are considering eliminating this behavior by making (theta > 0.99)
an illegal statement if theta is not data. Then we would be able to
tell what gets executed by running once because the data would never
change. This is something we're thinking about going forward.

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] 2 kinds of error checking
parts:
Shape (e.g., 2-dimensional array or row vector)
we test at compile time. Size (e.g., 5 x 3 array or
5-vector) we test at run time.

We do wind up doing some redundant tests, too. For
example, declaring lower=0 on a scale parameter sigma
specified as data will get tested as the data is loaded
and then each time it is used in normal().

In the densities, the size and sign tests are trivial
compared to the amount of work going on for autodiff.

- Bob
